Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

whatever pronoun

also anything that, no matter what, whatsoever

classical

Hor. Ep. 1.2.14: quidquid dēlīrant rēgēs, plectuntur Achīvī
Cic. Att. 12.1.2: garrīmus quicquid in buccam

quisquis, quicquid (quidquid)

relative pronoun, with a verb of its own

whatever, whoever

Both spellings of the neuter are ancient (Quint. 1.7.6). In its own Latin the house writes the assimilated quicquid, as the libellī do; quotations keep their edition’s spelling.

Other words

  • quīcumque, quaecumque, quodcumque — whatever, whichever (with a noun or alone)

    relative pronoun and adjective · also used · classical · Catull. 39.6–7: quodcumque agit; Caes. BG 1.31.14: fortūnam, quaecumque accidat, experiantur

    Cicero, Caesar and Sallust give it a verb of its own; “any … whatever” without one is Livy’s and later (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • quārē habē tibi quidquid hoc libellī quālecumque

    so take this little book for your own, whatever it is, such as it isCatull. 1.8–9

  • quidquid dēlīrant rēgēs, plectuntur Achīvī

    whatever madness the kings commit, the Greeks pay for itHor. Ep. 1.2.14

  • quidquid est, ubicumque est, quodcumque agit, renīdet

    whatever it is, wherever he is, whatever he is doing, he grinsCatull. 39.6–7

  • quidquid praecipiēs, estō brevis, ut citō dicta percipiant animī docilēs teneantque fidēlēs

    whatever you teach, be brief, so that minds may grasp what is said quickly, learn it and keep it faithfullyHor. AP 335–336

  • quid, cum cōram sumus et garrīmus quicquid in buccam?

    and what about when we are together and chatter whatever comes into our heads?Cic. Att. 12.1.2

See also whoever, whichever, what.
